text: [[e:palakus|Palakus]] was defeated around 110 BCE by [[e:diophantes|Diophantes]], general of [[e:mithridates-vi-of-pontus|Mithridates VI of Pontus]], and the kingdom lost its leading role. It survived in a weaker form, often in conflict with the [[s:bosporan-kingdom|Bosporan Kingdom]], until [[e:goths|Goths]] and other invaders destroyed [[s:neapolis|Neapolis]] in the mid 3rd century CE.

Saint Lucia remains a [[e:parliamentary-democracy|parliamentary democracy]] and Commonwealth realm. [[e:philip-j-pierre|Philip J. Pierre]] of the Labour Party became prime minister in 2021, and [[e:saint-lucian-creole|Kwéyòl]], French place names and Catholic traditions continue to shape national identity.

The federation remains a [[e:parliamentary-democracy|parliamentary democracy]] within the Commonwealth. [[e:terrance-drew|Terrance Drew]] became prime minister in 2022. Relations between [[e:saint-kitts|Saint Kitts]] and [[s:colony-of-nevis|Nevis]], and dependence on passport sales, continue to shape its politics.

King [[e:kilamuwa|Kilamuwa's]] inscription boasts that he hired the king of [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] against his enemies and improved the lot of his poor subjects. Later kings wrote in a local [[e:aramaic|Aramaic]] dialect; [[e:bar-rakib|Bar-Rakib]] built palaces as a loyal [[e:vassal|vassal]] of Tiglath-Pileser III. The [[e:kuttamuwa-stele|Kuttamuwa stele]], found in 2008, shows a belief in a soul dwelling in the stone.

[[e:shimazu-takahisa|Takahisa]]'s son [[e:shimazu-yoshihisa|Yoshihisa]] and his brothers [[e:shimazu-yoshihiro|Yoshihiro]], [[e:shimazu-toshihisa|Toshihisa]] and [[e:shimazu-iehisa|Iehisa]] formed a formidable military team. They conquered [[e:osumi-province|Osumi]] and [[e:hyuga-province|Hyuga]], crushed the [[e:otomo-clan|Otomo]] at [[e:battle-of-mimikawa|Mimikawa]] in 1578 and the [[e:ryuzoji-clan|Ryuzoji]] at [[e:battle-of-okitanawate|Okitanawate]] in 1584, and by 1586 controlled most of [[e:kyushu|Kyushu]]. The domain drew strength from a large warrior class and trade through its ports.
The vast southern kingdom of the middle Yangtze whose distinctive culture produced the poetry of Qu Yuan and which was Qin's most formidable rival.

The kings ruled a small, embattled realm, and their stelae speak of war and famine. [[e:neferhotep-iii|Neferhotep III]] and [[e:nebiryraw-i|Nebiryraw I]] are among the better-attested rulers; stelae of Neferhotep III boast of rescuing [[s:thebes|Thebes]] in a time of hunger. They relied on the god [[e:amun|Amun]] and local garrisons, and were pressed by both the [[s:fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt]] to the north and [[s:kerma|Kerma]] to the south.

Sirohi was a rugged state on the routes between [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] and [[s:jodhpur-state|Marwar]], often at war with Marwar. Its territory included [[e:mount-abu|Mount Abu]], with the marble [[e:dilwara-temples|Dilwara Jain temples]], and Sirohi blades were renowned across [[e:india|India]]. The state signed a treaty with the British in 1823, and in 1845 leased part of Mount Abu for a sanatorium, which became headquarters of the [[e:rajputana-agency|Rajputana Agency]].
The Theban kings who began the war that drove the Hyksos from Egypt and paved the way for the New Kingdom.

The [[e:peoples-action-party|People's Action Party]] has governed without interruption, combining elections with tight control of the press and opposition. The state attracted foreign manufacturers, built public housing for most citizens through the Housing and Development Board, and fostered a multiracial identity with English, Malay, [[e:mandarin-chinese|Mandarin]] and Tamil as official languages. Its port and airport became among the busiest in the world.

When [[e:shivaji-of-thanjavur|Shivaji II]] died in 1855 without a male heir, the British annexed [[e:thanjavur|Thanjavur]] under the doctrine of lapse. The palace, library and the painting style it fostered survive in Thanjavur.

[[e:mixtecs|Mixtec]] kingdoms were small [[e:city-state|city-states]] ruled by lords and ladies of interlinked noble houses, and Tilantongo was considered the senior line. In the 11th century [[e:eight-deer-jaguar-claw|Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw]], a lord from Tilantongo, built a wide domain through war and alliance before being sacrificed in 1115. Mixtec artisans were renowned for gold work, turquoise mosaic and painted books.

The emperor (tsenpo) ruled through powerful noble clans and ministers; a [[e:census|census]] and military districts underpinned a formidable cavalry army. Writing in a script based on Indian models is credited to [[e:songtsen-gampo|Songtsen Gampo's]] reign. [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] conquered the [[s:tuyuhun|Tuyuhun]] in 663, contested the [[e:tarim-basin|Tarim Basin]] with [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China]], briefly occupied [[e:changan|Chang'an]] in 763 and held [[e:dunhuang|Dunhuang]]. [[e:trisong-detsen|Trisong Detsen]] made [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] the state religion and founded [[e:samye|Samye]] monastery.
The first regional government of Transcaucasia after the October Revolution, which refused to recognise Bolshevik power and paved the way for independence.

In the 3rd and 4th centuries the area was disrupted by Frankish raids. In 358 the future emperor Julian accepted the submission of the [[s:salian-franks|Salian Franks]], who had already settled in [[e:toxandria|Toxandria]], and let them stay as Roman allies, and the region became the cradle of Frankish power in the [[e:low-countries|Low Countries]].
The late Tang military circuit in northern Vietnam whose local governors, the Khuc family, laid the groundwork for Vietnamese independence.
A large chiefdom at the meeting of the Tapajós and Amazon rivers, known for its intricate pottery and dark earth soils.

From 1881 the [[e:mahdi|Mahdi]], [[e:muhammad-ahmad|Muhammad Ahmad]], led a revolt against Egyptian rule. His forces took [[e:khartoum|Khartoum]] in January 1885, killing [[e:charles-george-gordon|Gordon]], and founded the [[s:mahdist-state|Mahdist State]]. The Turkiyya left [[e:sudan|Sudan]] with its capital, much of its territory and a lasting legacy of the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]].
A short-lived union of Tuscany, Modena, Parma and Romagna formed in 1859, which voted to join Piedmont and paved the way for Italian unity.
The Kashmir dynasty of Avantivarman, whose engineer Suyya tamed the Jhelum and whose court fostered great Sanskrit literary theory.

The sultans ruled a large but thinly populated territory of wadis and highland plateaus, where the Aulaqi were known as formidable fighters, many serving abroad as soldiers. The sultanate entered British protection by treaty and formed part of the [[s:aden-protectorate|Aden Protectorate]]. It joined the [[s:federation-of-south-arabia|Federation of South Arabia]] in the 1960s.

Vulci was a major centre of [[e:bronze-working|bronze-working]], exporting tripods, vessels and candelabra across [[e:italy|Italy]] and beyond the [[e:alps|Alps]]. Its tombs yielded an extraordinary number of Athenian painted vases, many excavated by [[e:lucien-bonaparte|Lucien Bonaparte]] in the 19th century. The [[e:francois-tomb|François Tomb's]] paintings show the Vulcian heroes [[e:caelius-vibenna|Caile]] and [[e:aulus-vibenna|Avle Vipinas]] and [[e:mastarna|Macstrna]], whom the emperor [[e:claudius|Claudius]] identified with [[e:rome|Rome's]] king [[e:servius-tullius|Servius Tullius]].

Vala was founded around 1740 by a junior branch of the [[e:gohil|Gohil Rajputs]] who ruled [[s:bhavnagar-state|Bhavnagar State]]. Its town, Vala or Vallabhipur, lay at the site of ancient [[e:valabhi|Valabhi]], capital of the [[e:maitraka-dynasty|Maitraka]] kingdom and a renowned Buddhist and Jain centre of learning.

According to the sagas, [[e:halfdan-the-black|Halfdan the Black]] extended Vestfold's power over the [[e:upplands-norway|Upplands]], and his son [[e:harald-fairhair|Harald Fairhair]] conquered western [[e:norway|Norway]], traditionally at [[e:battle-of-hafrsfjord|Hafrsfjord]] around 872. Vestfold thus became the cradle of the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]], and its ship burials are among the best-known finds of the [[e:viking-age|Viking Age]].

From its capital Wari established planned provincial centres such as [[e:pikillacta|Pikillacta]] near [[e:cusco|Cusco]], [[e:viracochapampa|Viracochapampa]] in the north and [[e:cerro-baul|Cerro Baúl]] in [[e:moquegua|Moquegua]], facing [[s:tiwanaku|Tiwanaku]]. These rectangular compounds suggest a centralised administration that controlled labour and goods. Wari built terraces and roads that the [[e:inca-empire|Incas]] later reused, and may have used early [[e:quipu|khipus]] for records. Its tapestry tunics and colourful pottery spread a common style. Tombs at [[e:el-castillo-de-huarmey|El Castillo de Huarmey]] show the wealth of Wari noblewomen.

They controlled the rich port of [[e:bharuch|Bharuch]] and the trade routes to [[e:ujjain|Ujjain]]. Their [[e:silver|silver]] coins, dated in the [[e:saka-era|Saka era]] from 78, give an unusually exact chronology. [[e:rudradaman-i|Rudradaman I's]] [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]] inscription of 150 boasts of his victories over the [[s:satavahana-dynasty|Satavahana dynasty]] and the [[s:yaudheya-republic|Yaudheyas]] and of repairing the [[e:sudarshana-lake|Sudarshana]] reservoir, and is written in elegant [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]], a sign of its spread as a courtly language.

The Concessions and Agreements of 1677, associated with [[e:william-penn|Penn]], guaranteed freedom of conscience, [[e:jury-trial|trial by jury]] and an elected assembly with wide powers. [[e:quakers|Quaker]] meetings shaped community life, and the colony served as a model for the [[s:province-of-pennsylvania|Province of Pennsylvania]]. Farmers along the [[e:delaware-river|Delaware]] raised grain and livestock. After [[e:edward-byllynge|Byllynge]]'s death the physician [[e:daniel-coxe|Daniel Coxe]] bought the governing rights in 1687 and sold them to the West [[s:bailiwick-of-jersey|Jersey]] Society in 1692.

The Yaudheyas were a gana governed by an assembly and an elected leader. Their coins carry the legend Yaudheya ganasya jaya, victory to the Yaudheya republic, and images of [[e:kartikeya|Karttikeya]], the war god they treated as their divine sovereign. Their reputation for military skill was such that the [[s:saka|Saka]] ruler Rudradaman boasted in his [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]] inscription of 150 of having defeated them.

US Secretary of State John Hay pressed the great powers to grant equal trading rights in China and respect its territorial integrity. The Open Door became a cornerstone of American policy in East Asia.

After a five-month siege, Robert Guiscard and his brother Roger took Palermo from its Muslim rulers. The conquest paved the way for the Norman Kingdom of Sicily, a meeting place of Latin, Greek and Arab cultures.

On the death of Tsar Alexei, his sickly 14-year-old son Feodor succeeded him. In a short reign he abolished the system of ranking nobles by ancestry, paving the way for his half-brother Peter the Great.
Proclaimed emperor by his troops at Chenqiao, the general became Emperor Taizu of Song. The dynasty reunited most of China and presided over remarkable advances in commerce, printing and technology.
The Central Committee accepted Mikhail Gorbachev's proposal to end the party's constitutional leading role. The change opened the way to multi-party politics in the Soviet Union.
Legendary founding of Japan by Emperor Jimmu
Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Supreme Court could strike down acts of Congress that conflicted with the Constitution. The decision became a cornerstone of American constitutional law.

The Ostrogothic king Vitiges ended the siege of Rome, which Byzantine forces under General Belisarius had held against his numerically superior army since March 537. The siege, the first major clash of the Gothic War, played a decisive role in its course.
Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg agreed to defend one another against attack. The pact paved the way for NATO in 1949 and later became the Western European Union.

Two hundred noblemen led by Hendrick van Brederode forced their way to the regent Margaret of Parma with a petition seeking to moderate the placards against heresy. The petition played a crucial role in the events leading to the Dutch Revolt.

The Ottoman sultan Mehmed II laid siege to Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire. After 53 days, in which heavy artillery played a major role, the city fell on 29 May, ending the Byzantine Empire and becoming the Ottoman capital.
Cromwell entered the Commons with musketeers and expelled the remaining members. The act paved the way for his rule as Lord Protector later that year.

A law of the Consulate maintained slavery where it had not been abolished and paved the way for its return elsewhere, reversing the Revolution's abolition of 1794. Resistance helped drive Haiti to independence.

Ptolemy IV Philopator of Egypt defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus III the Great near present-day Rafah in the Fourth Syrian War, with native Egyptian troops playing a significant role. The battle determined the sovereignty of Coele-Syria.

Thebans under Epaminondas, with their allies, defeated the Spartans, Eleans, Athenians and Mantineans in a battle to decide which alliance would dominate Greece. Epaminondas died, and both sides were weakened, paving the way for Philip II of Macedon.

Bernardo de Irigoyen for Argentina and Francisco de Borja Echeverría for Chile signed a treaty in Buenos Aires to fix a precise border. Though it divided largely unexplored lands, it laid the groundwork for nearly all of today's 5600 km border.
By heating mercuric oxide, Joseph Priestley produced a gas in which a candle burned with remarkable vigour. He called it 'dephlogisticated air'; Lavoisier later named it oxygen.
The cornerstone of the pedestal was laid on Bedloe's Island in New York Harbor. Americans had to raise the funds for the base, while France paid for the statue itself.
Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act, creating old-age pensions, unemployment insurance and aid for dependent children. It became the cornerstone of the American welfare state.
Diana was fatally injured when her car crashed in the Pont de l'Alma tunnel while pursued by photographers. Her death provoked an extraordinary outpouring of public grief in Britain and beyond.
At 4.50 am all traffic in Sweden stopped, changed sides and restarted on the right. Dagen H, 'H Day', went remarkably smoothly after years of preparation.
George Washington lays the cornerstone of the US Capitol
President Washington laid the cornerstone of the Capitol in a Masonic ceremony. Congress first met in the unfinished building in November 1800.
The cornerstone of the White House is laid
Freemasons laid the cornerstone of the President's House in the new federal city of Washington. Designed by James Hoban, it has housed every US president since John Adams.

Jadwiga, youngest daughter of Louis I of Hungary, was crowned king of Poland, rather than queen, to highlight her sovereign status. Under the Union of Krewo she later married the Lithuanian grand duke Jogaila, beginning the dynastic union of Poland and Lithuania.

With crusader help, Afonso I, the first king of Portugal, ended a siege begun on 1 July and took Lisbon from the Moors. The siege, seen as pivotal in the Reconquista, was one of the few Christian victories of the Second Crusade.

Irene of Athens, sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire since 797, was overthrown by her General Logothete, Nikephoros, who seized the throne; she was banished to Lesbos. Her five years of sole rule had been unprecedented in Roman and Byzantine history.

An Abbasid army under Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Katib defeated pro-Isma'ili Bedouin near Hama in Syria, capturing and executing their leaders. The victory paved the way for the Abbasid reconquest of the Tulunid domains in southern Syria and Egypt.

The Council of People's Commissars of the Russian SFSR set up the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission, the Cheka, the first Soviet secret police, under Felix Dzerzhinsky. By the end of the Russian Civil War in 1922 it had at least 200,000 personnel.

"Abide with Me" is a Christian hymn by the Anglican cleric Henry Francis Lyte (1793–1847). Lyte was a curate in County Wexford from 1815 to 1818, where he often preached at the church in Killurin and came under the lasting influence of its rector, the Reverend Abraham Swanne; he was later vicar of All Saints' Church in Brixham, Devon. In poor health for most of his life, he travelled abroad for relief, as was usual at the time. The hymn takes its starting point from Luke 24:29, where the disciples ask Jesus to abide with them "for it is toward evening and the day is far spent".

The date of the text is disputed. An article in The Spectator of 3 October 1925 said that Lyte wrote it in 1820, while staying with the Hore family in County Wexford, after sitting with a dying friend, William Augustus Le Hunte, who kept repeating the words "abide with me"; on this account Lyte recalled those lines twenty-seven years later, when he was dying of tuberculosis. The usual date is 1847. His daughter, Anna Maria Maxwell Hogg, told how in September of that year, against his family's fears, he preached once more to his people, and that evening gave a near relative the little hymn with an air of his own composing. Lyte died weeks later, on 20 November 1847, in Nice, then in the Kingdom of Sardinia, and the hymn was first sung at his funeral.

The tune most often sung is not Lyte's but "Eventide", written in 1861 by the English organist William Henry Monk, the first editor of Hymns Ancient and Modern; one edition of that hymnal left out a verse about the singer's youth as too personal. Other tunes followed, among them Samuel Liddle's setting of 1896, the one Dame Clara Butt favoured. Ralph Vaughan Williams wrote a descant for the hymnal Songs of Praise (1925) and an orchestral prelude on Eventide for the Hereford Festival of 1936, and Charles Ives set the hymn around 1890.

The hymn is sung in many Christian denominations, and King George V and Mahatma Gandhi were said to hold it a favourite. It is often sung at funerals: those of Sun Yat-sen in 1925, of George V in 1936, of Queen Mary in 1953, of Jean, Grand Duke of Luxembourg, in 2019 and of Harald V of Norway in 2026. It was sung at the burial of the Unknown Warrior in Westminster Abbey in 1920, and is sometimes sung on Anzac Day in Australia and New Zealand and on Remembrance Day in Canada and the United Kingdom.

Its first and last verses are sung at the FA Cup Final about 15 minutes before kick-off. The custom may go back to the 1923 final between Bolton Wanderers and West Ham United, when the event choir sang it while crowds were cleared from the pitch; its first formal use was at the 1927 final between Arsenal and Cardiff City, and it has been sung before every Rugby League Challenge Cup Final since 1929. Emeli Sandé sang it at the opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics, in tribute to the victims of the 7/7 terrorist attacks. Thelonious Monk recorded an arrangement in 1957, and in 2019 the programme Songs of Praise named it the fifth most popular hymn among British Christians.

The Akathist Hymn takes its name from the Greek for "unseated": while it is chanted, the congregation stands in reverence, and only the aged and the infirm sit. In Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic services, where sitting, standing and bowing follow intricate rules, standing is required of all only for the Gospel, the Six Psalms of Matins and the akathists. The hymn par excellence is the one addressed to the Theotokos, the Mother of God, for the feast of the Annunciation on 25 March. It was long attributed to Romanos the Melodist, whose kontakia dominated the repertoire sung at Hagia Sophia, but recent scholarship rejects his authorship. Others have named Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople, or, as J. M. Quercius argued in 1777, George Pisida, deacon and sacristan of Hagia Sophia, whose poems echo it in style and theme. No certain author can be named.

The Synaxarion ties the feast to the year 626, when Constantinople, in the reign of Heraclius, was attacked by the Persians and the Avars and was saved, it says, by the Theotokos; it also credits her with two later victories, under Leo III the Isaurian and Constantine Pogonatus. The link was disputed on the grounds that the hymn could not have been written in a day and that its twenty-four stanzas never allude to such a siege. Before the 21st century the hymn was usually placed in the 6th or 7th century; Leena Peltomaa argued from its theology for the 5th century, and most scholars now favour an early date, somewhere between the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon or, in another view, the later 5th or early 6th century. Its closing kontakion addresses Mary as the saviour of Constantinople in the siege of 626, and the hymn also served to celebrate military victories and to ask for divine protection in war.

The hymn is an alphabetical acrostic: its twenty-four oikoi, or stanzas, each begin with the next letter of the Greek alphabet. Twelve long oikoi end in long chains of greetings, the chairetismoi, each line starting "Rejoice" and the whole closing with a refrain to Mary as the unwedded bride; the twelve short ones end in Alleluia. The work is divided into thirteen parts of a kontakion and an oikos each. Even the earliest chant books with musical notation, such as the Tipografsky Ustav, write out all twenty-four oikoi, though they give music only for the first.

Since the 14th century the Akathist has belonged to the season of Lent. Divided into four parts by theme (the Annunciation, the Nativity, Christ and the Theotokos herself), it is sung at the service of the Salutations to the Theotokos on the first four Friday evenings of Great Lent and whole on the fifth, and it is included in the Matins of the fifth Saturday of Lent, the "Saturday of the Akathist"; the service is called Chairetismoi in Greek and Madayeh in Arabic. In monasteries of the Athonite tradition the whole hymn is sung nightly at Compline. In the Slavic churches the akathist grew into a genre of its own, with many newer akathists to saints modelled on the old one, while the Greek, Arabic and Russian Old Rite traditions allow only the original in formal worship. Three icons of the Theotokos on Mount Athos bear its name: at the Dionysiou Monastery, a gift of the Emperor Alexios III Komnenos, which tradition says Patriarch Sergius carried around the walls of Constantinople in 626; at Hilandar, where the icon was untouched by a fire in 1837 while the monks chanted the Akathist before it; and at Zographou.

After the May Revolution of 1810, poets and musicians in Buenos Aires wrote a number of patriotic songs. The earliest, a "Patriotic March" published anonymously on 15 November 1810 in the Gazeta de Buenos Ayres, is generally believed to have words by Esteban de Luca and music by Blas Parera; it did not mention Argentina or any independent state. In mid-1812 the ruling triumvirate had the Buenos Aires Cabildo commission a national song: a text by the Franciscan friar Cayetano Rodríguez was approved on 4 August, and Parera, the music director of the local theatre, set it and conducted its premiere on 1 November.

Within a year the Assembly of Year XIII judged that song not effective enough, and the army's recent victories had made its words out of date. On 6 March 1813 several poets were invited to submit texts, and the poem by the lawyer Vicente López y Planes was chosen unanimously. On 11 May 1813 it was designated the sole national march, and it was published as a broadside three days later. Parera wrote new music within a few days. An unconfirmed tradition places the first performance on 14 May 1813 in the home of Mariquita Sánchez de Thompson; Parera conducted the official premiere in the theatre on 28 May and was paid 200 pesos. He may have shown his dislike of the new nation by quoting, in a minor key and with dissonant chords, a gesture from an anti-Napoleonic war song.

The text was fiercely pro-independence and anti-Spanish, and its outlook reached beyond Argentina to the struggles in Mexico, Central America, northern South America and Charcas, while its allegory cast not only Spanish absolutism but Spain itself as the enemy. A disputed word in one line, changed in a corrected song-sheet bearing the same date, reverses whether Buenos Aires sets itself against the other provinces or at their head; the first reading has been seen as a sign of the city's centralist views and also as a misprint. The song spread fast: within ten years it was performed throughout Argentina and also in Chile, Peru and Colombia, where it was used until those countries had anthems of their own. It was known as the "Canción Patriótica Nacional" and then the "Canción Patriótica"; the title "Himno Nacional Argentino" first appears on Juan Pedro Esnaola's arrangement of about 1848.

So many versions grew up that singing together became difficult. In 1860 Esnaola was commissioned to prepare an official version, with a slower tempo, a fuller texture and richer harmony. A committee's revision of 1927 that undid some of his changes was rejected after a public debate led by the newspaper La Prensa, and Esnaola's edition was confirmed as the official anthem in 1944; Decree 10302/1944 still governs it. Once hostility to Spain had faded and many Spanish immigrants had settled in the country, President Julio Argentino Roca decreed on 30 March 1900 that at official and public festivals and in schools only the first and last verses and the chorus should be sung, so no anti-Spanish text is sung today.

The anthem is performed at all official events, where those present stand and sing; radio stations play it at midnight, and on national holidays it must be played then. At international sporting events usually only the instrumental introduction, or a shortened form, is played. The rock musician Charly García caused controversy in 1990 with an idiosyncratic version on his album Filosofía barata y zapatos de goma, which broke the regulations on reproducing the anthem. Argentina celebrates National Anthem Day on 11 May.

"Arirang" is a Korean folk song that exists in about 3,600 variations of 60 different versions, all sharing a refrain built on the word "arirang", which has no precise meaning in Korean. It is thought to be more than 600 years old. The usual view, held by Professor Keith Howard and by the Academy of Korean Studies, is that it began as a folk song of the mountains of Jeongseon in Gangwon Province; its first mention is in a manuscript of 1756, and some people of Jeongseon trace it back to the Goryeo era. A local legend ties it to two lovers who met while picking camellia blossoms near the water of Auraji: in one telling the young man could not cross the high water and the two sang of their sorrow, in another he drowned trying. Scholars have offered many explanations of the name, among them "my beloved one" (Shin Yong-ha), "long hill" (Yang Ju-dong) and a link with Lady Aryeong, wife of the first king of Silla.

One account holds that the song spread to Seoul and the rest of Korea when workers from Gangwon were sent to rebuild Gyeongbok Palace under the Prince Regent Heungseon; some trace the words of its refrain to the cries of their families as the officials took them away. The scholar Hwang Hyeon's record, the Maecheonyarok, suggests the song was widespread by then. The first known recording was made in 1896 by the American ethnologist Alice C. Fletcher, who recorded three Korean singers at her home in Washington, D.C.; who they were (students at Howard University from noble families, or Korean workers) is uncertain. The recording is in the Library of Congress.

Under Japanese rule, singing patriotic songs, Korea's national anthem among them, became a crime, and "Arirang" became an unofficial anthem of resistance. Protesters sang it during the March First Movement of 1919, and mountain guerrillas fighting the occupiers sang it too. Many versions written in these years speak of injustice, the hardship of labourers and guerrilla war, and several were banned in the 1930s for "disturbance of public order". The best-known words first appeared in Na Woon-gyu's silent film Arirang (1926), now lost, which by various accounts told of a Korean student driven mad by imprisonment and torture under the Japanese; it is considered the first Korean nationalist film. Its theme, "Bonjo Arirang" (Standard Arirang) from Seoul, became the most famous version, beside "Jeongseon Arirang", generally held to be the original, "Jindo Arirang" from South Jeolla and "Miryang Arirang" from South Gyeongsang.

Korean emigrants took the song to Japan from the 1910s, and between 1931 and 1943 more than 50 Japanese versions were released, in pop, jazz and mambo. The Okinawan version keeps more of its folk character. Yonaha Hirotoshi, who as a boy had heard it sung by Korean women forced into sexual slavery by the Japanese army ("comfort women"), built an Arirang monument in Miyakojima in 2008.

After the division of Korea the song is sung in both North and South and serves as a symbol of the unity of the two states. At the opening of the 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, athletes of both Koreas entered together under the Korean Unification Flag to "Arirang". The U.S. Army's 7th Infantry Division, stationed in South Korea from 1950 to 1971, took it as its march in May 1956 with the permission of President Syngman Rhee. China added it to its national list of intangible cultural heritage in 2011, and in 2023 the ethnic Korean singer Cui Liling published a variation on Heaven Lake for the 70th anniversary of Yanbian's Korean autonomous region. South Korea (2012) and North Korea (2014) each had it inscribed on UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage, and in 2015 South Korea's Cultural Heritage Administration listed it as an important intangible cultural asset.

"Bhaja Govindam" ("praise Govinda", or "seek Govinda"), also called "Moha Mudgara" ("destroyer of illusion"), is a popular Hindu devotional poem in Sanskrit traditionally attributed to Adi Shankara. Its opening stanza is a refrain repeated after each verse, as Swami Chinmayananda describes it. The twelve verses after it, the Dvadasa-manjarika-stotram, are traditionally Shankara's own; fourteen more, the Caturdasa-manjarika-stotram, are attributed to fourteen of his disciples. Editions differ in the number, order, wording and arrangement of the stanzas, but not in their meaning. The poem is written in a moraic metre, measured in syllabic instants (mātrās) rather than a fixed number of syllables: apart from the first verse, every verse has sixteen mātrās, the padakulakam of the metrical handbook Vrtta-ratnakara.

A traditional story tells how it came to be. Walking with his disciples along a street in Varanasi, Shankara met an old scholar reciting the rules of Panini's Sanskrit grammar over and over. Taking pity on him, he advised the man not to spend his last years on grammar but to turn his mind to God in worship, which alone could free him from the cycle of birth and death; the hymn is said to have been composed then. It shows that Shankara, often regarded as the reviver of the path of knowledge (jnana marga) to liberation, also taught the path of devotion (bhakti marga), the emphasis of the bhakti movement. In his commentary C. Rajagopalachari wrote that knowledge which has matured is spoken of as devotion, and that knowledge which does not become devotion is "useless tinsel". Many scholars hold that the poem sums up, briefly and simply, the substance of Shankara's Vedantic thought, and because its refrain invokes God as Krishna it is sung not only by Shankara's own followers, the Smarthas, but also by Vaishnavas and others.

The Cantigas de Santa Maria ("Canticles of Holy Mary") are 420 poems with musical notation, written in medieval Galician-Portuguese at the court of Alfonso X of Castile, called El Sabio, "the Wise" (1221-1284). Tradition attributes them all to Alfonso, but scholars have established that the poets and musicians of his court wrote most of them, with the king credited with a few: he names himself in the first person, and the collection's prologue supports his part. Several studies suggest that the Galician poet Airas Nunes may have written a large number. It is one of the largest collections of monophonic (solo) songs to survive from the Middle Ages.

Alfonso's workshops wrote their histories and other prose in Castilian, but the Cantigas are in Galician-Portuguese, which was then fashionable as a language of lyric poetry in Castile; Alfonso had also spent part of his early years in Galicia and probably spoke it from childhood. The collection reflects the popularity at his court of other Galician-Portuguese poetry, the cantigas d'amigo and cantigas d'amor.

Every song mentions the Virgin Mary. Of the 420, 356 are narratives of Marian miracles; the others, apart from an introduction and two prologues, are songs of praise or for Marian feasts, and every tenth song is a hymn. The miracle songs show Mary in a very human way, often taking part in earthly episodes, and many speak of devotion to her in the language of the troubadours' courtly love. The verse forms are extraordinarily varied, 280 different formats for 420 songs, most often the virelai and the rondeau, with lines of two to 24 syllables. The music is written in a notation like that of chant but with some indication of note lengths; its rhythm remains a lively subject of debate.

The songs survive in four codices, thought to have been made in Alfonso's lifetime: the Toledo codex (To, now in the National Library in Madrid), the earliest, with 129 songs, perhaps from the 1270s; the "codex of the musicians" (E, El Escorial), the fullest, with 406 songs and miniatures of pairs of musicians playing a wide variety of instruments; the richly illustrated Códice Rico (T, El Escorial), with 195 surviving songs, each shown in six or twelve narrative pictures; and its unfinished sister volume in Florence (F), with 111, whose staves were never filled with music. T, F and E date from the early 1280s up to Alfonso's death in 1284.

The Cantigas are often performed and recorded by early-music groups, among them Eduardo Paniagua and Música Antigua, Federico Bardazzi and Ensemble San Felice, Esther Lamandier and Jordi Savall. Because the original notation is ambiguous, their recordings differ greatly from one another.

"Nelson Mandela", known in some versions as "Free Nelson Mandela", was written by the British musician Jerry Dammers and recorded by the band the Special A.K.A., with Stan Campbell singing lead. Dammers said he knew very little about Mandela until he went to an anti-apartheid concert in London in 1983, which gave him the idea for the song. At the time few people outside South Africa knew who Mandela was, and the British prime minister, Margaret Thatcher, had condemned him as a terrorist for his resistance to the South African government.

The song came out in 1984 as a single with "Break Down the Door" on the other side, produced by Elvis Costello. Molly and Polly Jackson, two girls the drummer John Bradbury had met in a bar in Camden, sang backing vocals, and session singers including Claudia Fontaine and Caron Wheeler sang the chorus. Unlike most protest songs it is upbeat and celebratory and draws on South African music. Campbell left the band after the recording and the video, and returned only for two appearances on the BBC's Top of the Pops in 1984.

The single reached number nine on the UK Singles Chart and was immensely popular in Africa. It was banned in South Africa, but, as Dammers recalled, it got back into the country and was played at football matches, which were communal gatherings of black South Africans, at other sporting events and at ANC rallies. The South African writer Jonny Steinberg credited it with spreading not only Mandela's name but what that name came to mean, and the broadcaster Paul Gambaccini put part of its weight down to the band's standing in Britain.

A remake for Mandela's 70th birthday tribute came out in 1988, with Elvis Costello, Dave Wakeling, Ranking Roger and Lynval Golding among the backing singers. At the tribute for his 90th birthday in London's Hyde Park in June 2008 the song closed the show, sung by Amy Winehouse. Since 1984 the students' union of Wadham College, Oxford, has ended every college dance with it. In March 2010 the New Statesman listed it among its "Top 20 Political Songs". After Mandela's death in December 2013 the single re-entered the UK chart at number 96, and in January 2014 Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band opened their first concert in South Africa, at the Bellville Velodrome in Cape Town, with it.

The Ghost Dance songs belong to a ceremony that began among the Northern Paiute of Mason Valley, in what became the state of Nevada. A typhoid epidemic in 1867, and other diseases more common among Europeans, had killed about one-tenth of the people, and the disruption had kept many families from their nomadic way of life. In 1869 the healer Hawthorne Wodziwob organised community dances to announce a vision of the land of the dead, helped by the "weather doctor" Tavibo. Tavibo's son Wovoka, also called Jack Wilson, was believed to have had a vision during the solar eclipse of 1 January 1889. According to the anthropologist James Mooney, who interviewed him before 1892, Wovoka taught that the people must love one another and not fight, must work and not steal or lie, and must give up war and the old self-mutilation of mourning; if the dance was performed for five days at the proper intervals, the living and the dead would be reunited. The Paiute called it "Dance In A Circle"; the Lakota name, "Spirit Dance", was translated as "Ghost Dance".

The dance grew out of the circle or round dance, in which large groups move in a ring, usually around a leader and often with singers. At its height a Ghost Dance drew hundreds of people, many from nearby reservations, who fasted for one or two days beforehand and went into sweat lodges, men and women apart. For two to four days the dancers held hands, faces turned upwards, and shuffled slowly sideways in a clockwise circle, singing Ghost Dance songs, while shamans waved eagle-wing fans before them; the dance itself used no instruments. Exhausted dancers fell unconscious into the centre and the circle closed behind them. The aim was a trance in which the dancer travelled to the afterworld and saw the times before the Europeans came, when bison were plentiful; on waking, dancers told the shamans what they had seen. Ella Cara Deloria and Elaine and Dora Goodale left eyewitness accounts.

The message spread quickly across much of the western United States, to California and Oklahoma, as peoples sent delegates to see the prophet and many returned as believers; each people joined parts of the ritual to its own beliefs. Among the Lakota it took a more millenarian turn: a renewed earth from which the white settlers would be rolled away. In 1890 Kicking Bear is believed to have brought them the ghost shirts, said to turn bullets. That February the United States government broke a treaty and divided the Great Sioux Reservation into five smaller reservations to make room for homesteaders, and later that year, after a failed harvest and with the bison almost wiped out, it cut the Lakota's rations by half, leaving them at risk of starvation. The Lakota turned to the Ghost Dance. The agents of the Bureau of Indian Affairs took fright; James McLaughlin called for troops and named Sitting Bull as the movement's leader, while the former agent Valentine McGillycuddy saw nothing extraordinary in the dances and warned that the troops themselves would bring trouble. Thousands of soldiers were sent. On 15 December 1890 Sitting Bull was arrested for failing to stop his people's dancing, and was shot dead in the exchange of fire that followed.

On 29 December 1890, at Wounded Knee Creek near the Pine Ridge Agency, soldiers trying to disarm the Miniconjou band of Spotted Elk opened fire, with carbines and Hotchkiss guns on the hill above the camp. Between 200 and 300 Lakota were massacred by US soldiers, most of them women and children; 25 soldiers died, many by their own side's fire. Twenty soldiers received the Medal of Honor, and none of the medals has been revoked, although Congress apologised for the massacre in 1990. After Wounded Knee open dancing declined for fear of further violence, but the ceremony did not end: it went underground, and Wovoka, Kicking Bear and Short Bull went on teaching. Not every people took it up; Navajo leaders called it "worthless words" in 1890.

Soon after the gramophone came on the market, a small set of Ghost Dance songs, gathered by James Mooney, was recorded and pressed in 1894, and the masters are held by the Library of Congress; who sang them is not known, possibly Mooney himself. An Edison Kinetoscope film of a "Sioux Ghost Dance" from the 1890s showed a fast dance with a drum, unlike the slow ceremony. During the occupation of Wounded Knee in 1973, Lakota men and women, Mary Brave Bird among them, danced the Ghost Dance on the site where their ancestors had been killed, and Leonard Crow Dog later recalled the songs they sang there. The Caddo still practise the Ghost Dance, and the ceremonies continue in private, their details kept among the participants.

"Giovinezza" ("Youth") was composed by the lawyer and composer Giuseppe Blanc in 1909 as "Il Commiato" ("Farewell"), a graduation song of the University of Turin. It became popular among Italian soldiers in the First World War, and as the "Inno degli Arditi" it was the hymn of the Arditi, an assault corps of the Royal Army whose members later joined the fascist movement in large numbers. Gabriele d'Annunzio's mass rallies in Fiume spread it further. The version sung during the March on Rome was arranged by G. Castaldo in 1921 on Blanc's score, with words by Marcello Manni. After the march Benito Mussolini commissioned Salvator Gotta to write new words, completed in 1924, which made youth and nationalism the themes of the hymn.

From 1924 to 1943 "Giovinezza" was the official hymn of the National Fascist Party and of the regime, and an unofficial national anthem of the Kingdom of Italy. Official regulations had the Royal March, the state's anthem, played before it, and some sources consider that "Giovinezza" displaced the Royal March in practice, to the dismay of King Victor Emmanuel III: the pairing became a symbol of the diarchy of king and dictator. It was played at sporting events, in films and at public gatherings on the slightest pretext, and those who did not join in, foreigners included, could be roughed up by the Blackshirts. In the 1930s it became the official anthem of the army, and the school day had to open with it or with "Balilla", the song of the regime's youth organisation, the Opera Nazionale Balilla. A faint recording played in the Chapel of the Fascist Martyrs at the Exhibition of the Fascist Revolution, and Italian radio closed each day's broadcasting with it.

The hymn followed the opening of the Fascist parliament in 1924, elected under the Acerbo Law. Beniamino Gigli recorded it in 1937; the recording was later left out of his complete edition issued by EMI. On 12 March 1939, the day of Pius XII's coronation, the papal Palatine Guard played it in an exchange of courtesies with the Italian guards, who answered with the papal hymn, an incident outside the ceremony and without the pope's knowledge. A German song set to the tune replaced "Giovinezza" with "Hitlerleute", and Japanese translations were made to mark the Tripartite Pact and used in Japan's overseas broadcasting.

The conductor Arturo Toscanini, who had stood as a Fascist candidate in 1919, refused to conduct it in Milan in 1922 and later at Bayreuth. Mussolini stayed away from the premiere of Puccini's Turandot at La Scala on 25 April 1926 because Toscanini would not play it first. When Toscanini refused again at a concert in Bologna in May 1931, Blackshirts assaulted him, and he left Italy until after the Second World War.

After Mussolini was ousted in 1943, Italian radio closed its broadcasts with the Royal March alone for the first time in 21 years. New words were drafted for the Italian Social Republic, whose unofficial anthem it became; the triumphant tone of the old words did not fit the civil war then being fought in Italy, and the hymn preceded the Nazi radio broadcast announcing that republic. After Italy's capitulation in 1943 the Allies suppressed the hymn. Italy had no national anthem until "Il Canto degli Italiani" was provisionally chosen on 12 October 1946, after Italy became a republic; it was made official by law on 4 December 2017.

"Glory to Hong Kong" is a protest anthem of the 2019–2020 Hong Kong protests. Since mass protests against the extradition bill broke out in early June 2019, demonstrators had sung songs such as "Do You Hear the People Sing?" from Les Misérables and "Sing Hallelujah to the Lord". A music composer and Cantonese lyricist writing under the pseudonym "Thomas dgx yhl", mainly a pop rock artist, set out to write a song of their own "to boost protesters' morale and unite people"; Beyond's "Boundless Oceans, Vast Skies" and "Glory Days", he said, had rhythms out of place at the protests. Drawing on "God Save the King", "The Star-Spangled Banner", the national anthem of Russia, the "Battle Hymn of the Republic" and Vivaldi's Gloria, he spent two months on the melody, working backwards from its last line, which gives the song its title. He posted an instrumental version and the words on 26 August 2019 to LIHKG, an online forum of pro-democracy Hongkongers, and revised the words on its users' suggestions, among them adding a motto of the protests.

A music video of protest scenes went up on YouTube on 31 August 2019 and spread within days; an orchestral video with a four-part chorus, posted on 11 September, reached 1.5 million views in a week, and versions followed in English, German, Japanese, French, Catalan, Taiwanese and Italian. The song was sung at most demonstrations from then on: at a sit-in at Prince Edward station on 6 September demanding footage of the police's attacks on passengers on 31 August, by Hong Kong football supporters at a World Cup qualifier against Iran on 10 September, when the Chinese anthem was booed, and that night by large crowds in more than a dozen shopping malls at 8:31 pm, a reference to 31 August 2019 and to the decision of the National People's Congress Standing Committee of 31 August 2014; secondary school students sang it in human chains. Commentators called it the anthem of the protests and the unofficial anthem of Hong Kong. Its composer said it could only be a protest song: there was no nation, so there could be no national anthem.

Reactions divided along political lines. The Los Angeles Times wrote that its Cantonese words affirmed a collective identity at the heart of the conflict, and Chow Po-chung of the Chinese University of Hong Kong that it united the protesters; the former Legislative Council president Jasper Tsang praised it as a professional production. Wen Wei Po, a state-owned paper controlled by the Hong Kong Liaison Office, called it on 12 September 2019 an anthem of Hong Kong independence that idealised violence, and an article by Carmen Poon in Ming Pao the next day called it a brainwashing song promoting independence. In September 2019 RTHK staff reported being told not to play it outside the news, and its director said the song was to be avoided as controversial, though a spokeswoman said it had not been banned; in Guangzhou the dissident Lai Rifu was arrested on 16 September after posting a video with the song as background music. A version with new words praising the police, "May Truth be Bestowed Upon Hong Kong", was reposted on Sina Weibo by the People's Daily and the Communist Youth League.

After the national security law of 2020, the government declared phrases of the song, above all the protest motto it contains, separatist and subversive, and schools were told not to allow it. Public performances drew police attention and prosecutions on charges such as obstruction or busking without a licence; in September 2022 a harmonica player who played it among the mourners for Queen Elizabeth II outside the British Consulate was arrested for sedition, and a year later an elderly busker was jailed for a month for playing it on the erhu. Because Google searches for Hong Kong's national anthem returned the song, it was played in error for Hong Kong teams at a rugby sevens match in Incheon in November 2022, at a powerlifting championship in Dubai and at an ice hockey match in Sarajevo in February 2023; Chief Executive John Lee called it closely connected with the 2019 violence and with advocacy of independence, and Google declined the government's request to change its results.

In June 2023 the government sought a court injunction against the song's words, melody and adaptations. The Court of First Instance refused, citing the chilling effect on freedom of expression, but on 8 May 2024 the Court of Appeal granted it, banning the broadcasting, performing, publishing or distribution of the song, with exceptions for academic and journalistic purposes. YouTube blocked 32 videos of it in Hong Kong while saying it shared concerns about free expression; the song was briefly removed from streaming platforms worldwide and, after a month of removals and re-uploads, restored.

"La Bamba" is a Mexican folk song from the state of Veracruz and an example of son jarocho, a style of the region that combines Spanish (Andalusian), Indigenous, Afro-Mexican and Afro-Caribbean musical elements. It is typically played on one or two arpas jarochas (harps) with the jarana jarocha and the requinto jarocho, both string instruments. Its tune stays the same, but its words vary greatly, because performers often improvise verses as they play; versions by popular groups such as Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán and Los Pregoneros del Puerto have survived because of their fame.

The song is said to have begun as satire on the late and futile efforts of the viceroy of Mexico to defend the people of the port of Veracruz from pirates. His ships were old and leaky, and in the song a young sailor frantically works the pump, boasting that he, who keeps the ship afloat, is really its captain; the fast rhythm and hand movements of the dance comically imitate pumping water. The name also recalls a Spanish dance called bamba, popular at the time, which sounds close to bomba, a pump. The oldest known references to the song come from the town of Alvarado. Other explanations of the name, none certain, link it to the Spanish verb bambolear, "to sway", or to Africa through the slave trade: to the Bamba people of Central Africa or the Bambara of West Africa.

In a traditional version performed at weddings and in ballet folklórico shows, couples use intricate footwork to tie a bow that stands for their union. The custom of improvising verses comes from here: wedding guests were encouraged to make the song their own for the newlyweds, though verses taken as insults could start fights, and even the drawing of weapons.

The oldest known recording was made by Álvaro Hernández Ortiz, under the name El Jarocho, and released by Victor Records in Mexico in 1938 or 1939. According to a 1945 article in Life, the American bandleader Everett Hoagland brought the song and its dance to Ciro's nightclub in Mexico City, where it became popular; the presidential candidate Miguel Alemán Valdés adopted it for his successful campaign, and later in 1945 Arthur Murray introduced the music and dance at the Stork Club in New York City. Andrés Huesca and his brother Victor recorded a popular version around 1945–46, and the song appeared in the Mexican film Rayando el Sol (1946) and the MGM musical Fiesta (1947). In the 1950s the folk singers William Clauson and Cynthia Gooding recorded it in the United States.

Ritchie Valens learned the song as a boy from his cousin Dickie Cota. Proud of his Mexican heritage, he at first hesitated to merge it with rock and roll, fearing to commercialise a folk song; he spoke little Spanish and learned the words by sound. His 1958 rock and roll version, issued by Del-Fi as the B-side of "Donna", became a top 40 hit in the United States, and it is the only song not in English on Rolling Stone's list of the 500 greatest songs of all time. In 2018 the Library of Congress chose it for the National Recording Registry. Los Lobos recorded the song for La Bamba, the 1987 film of Valens's life, ending with a coda in the traditional style of Veracruz; their version topped the Billboard Hot 100.

"Le Temps des cerises" ("The Time of Cherries") is a French song written in 1866, with words by Jean-Baptiste Clément and music by Antoine Renard. It became very well known throughout the French-speaking countries.

The song came to be closely linked with the Paris Commune. Verses were added to it during the Commune, and it was sung from then on as a revolutionary song: the "time of cherries" was read as an image of life as it would be once a revolution had changed social and economic conditions. Clément is believed to have dedicated it to a nurse who fought in the Bloody Week (semaine sanglante), when French government troops overthrew the Commune.

Many versions of the words exist. The one most often heard today is the version popularised by the singer Yves Montand; Marc Ogeret, Juliette Gréco, Cora Vaucaire and Charles Trenet are among the others who recorded it, and Bobbejaan Schoepen sang it with Geike Arnaert of Hooverphonic.

The song has remained a symbol of the left. The Communist Party of Bohemia and Moravia took two cherries into its logo because of it, the French Communist Party adopted a new logo inspired by it in 2018, and it served as a symbol of The Left, a political party in Luxembourg. The town hall clock of Saint-Denis, a suburb of Paris, plays it for its hourly chime, alternating with "Le roi Dagobert a mis sa culotte à l'envers". In the film Porco Rosso the character Madame Gina sings it in a cabaret.

The "Lied der Partei" (Song of the Party), also known as "Die Partei hat immer recht" (The Party Is Always Right), was the anthem of the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED), the ruling party of East Germany. Its words and music were written in 1949 by the German-Bohemian Louis Fürnberg (1909–1957), who had joined the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia in 1928, and it was first performed in 1950.

Though the song spread as a hymn of praise, above all in East Germany, the occasion for it was the opposite. Fürnberg, then living in Prague, was not invited to the Ninth Congress of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia in 1949 because he was regarded as a German, which deeply hurt him. His widow, Lotte Fürnberg, explained in 2001 that he wrote the song to call himself back to order and to justify the slight to himself. The German article notes that, read closely, the lines show not only demonstrative obedience to the party in the climate of denunciation of the time but also a desperate defiance; years later Fürnberg told his wife that the song would one day do him great harm.

The cult of the party that the song expresses is regarded as typical of Leninism, which declared the Communist party the vanguard of the working class. The song also carried the personality cult of Joseph Stalin, who was named in its chorus. After the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in February 1956, with a more critical view of Stalin's rule, the text was altered. After the 22nd Congress, from November 1961 the Stalin cult was no longer part of East Germany's state ideology, and Stalin's name was removed from the song altogether (by 1964 according to the English article, from 1965 according to the German one).

By the Honecker era at the latest, "The Party is always right" had become a common saying in the GDR. In 1961 the writer Ralph Giordano, who had followed Stalinism until about 1955, used the phrase as the title of a book settling accounts with it. Since its founding in 2004 the German satirical party Die PARTEI has used a version with altered words as its "final party anthem".

The melody of "Lillibullero" is attributed to Henry Purcell, though it is unclear whether he composed it or arranged it; it was first published in The Delightful Companion, John Playford's method book for the recorder, in 1686, and no original manuscript survives. In the same year Thomas, Lord Wharton, wrote words to it satirising James II's appointment of the Catholic Richard Talbot, 1st Earl of Tyrconnell, as Lord Deputy of Ireland. The song is a mocking dialogue between two Irishmen about Talbot's arrival and what it would mean for the Protestants, who feared a massacre like that of the Irish Rebellion of 1641, when "Lilliburlero" had been a watchword of the Irish Catholics. Its nonsense refrain has been read as garbled Irish, perhaps alluding to a prophecy of the astrologer William Lilly; the song mocks both Irish faith in prophecy and English trust in Providence.

At first it made little impression. When James II began moving Irish regiments to England in 1688, the words were printed as broadsides, and by October the song was immensely popular, sung in the streets and especially in English barracks to mock the arriving Irish soldiers. The Whigs all but adopted it as their anthem in the Glorious Revolution. When William of Orange invaded the next month it was everywhere, said to be sung even by James's own palace guards, and a second part, rougher still, followed as William advanced. Wharton boasted that he had "sung a deluded Prince out of three kingdoms". Parodies answered it, among them an anti-Dutch song in circulation by 17 November.

The tune long outlived the quarrel. John Gay used it in The Beggar's Opera in 1728; Laurence Sterne printed its score in Tristram Shandy, where Uncle Toby whistles it; it carried the English drinking song "Nottingham Ale", sung at the launch of the East Indiaman Nottingham in 1787, and a nursery rhyme. In Ulster it became the tune of "Protestant Boys", played by flute bands at Orange Order parades, which were a subject of controversy during the Troubles. In the Second World War the BBC used it for the programme Into Battle, and it became the unofficial march of the British Army's Commandos; the BBC World Service then used it for decades as its interval signal before the news, chosen by engineers who found it carried well through short-wave noise, until a new theme by David Lowe was introduced in 2008; a shortened version is still sometimes played before the hourly news. It is the regimental march of the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers and of their Canadian and Australian counterparts.

"Personent hodie" is a Christmas carol first published in 1582 in Piae Cantiones, a Finnish song book of 74 medieval songs with Latin texts, collected by Jacobus Finno (Jaakko Suomalainen), a Lutheran cleric, and published by T. P. Rutha. The book grew out of the libraries of cathedral song schools, whose repertory had strong links with medieval Prague, where clerical students from Finland and Sweden had studied for generations. A highly similar melody is found in a manuscript of 1360 from the Bavarian city of Moosburg, and the song is usually dated from that manuscript.

The Latin text is probably a parody, in the musical sense, of a 12th-century song beginning "Intonent hodie voces ecclesie", written in honour of Saint Nicholas, patron saint of sailors and children, whose feast is 6 December. Hugh Keyte and Andrew Parrott point out that two of the verses have an unusual double repeat of a syllable. In the older song these repeats illustrated the three boys and the three girls whom Saint Nicholas saved, the boys from drowning and the girls from prostitution. The text was probably rewritten for the Feast of the Holy Innocents, 28 December, when the choristers and their "boy bishop" traditionally took the places of the senior clergy in the choir stalls. The carol is still often linked with Holy Innocents' Day.

Songs from Piae Cantiones went on being sung in Finland until the 19th century. In Britain the book became known after a rare copy, once owned by Peter of Nyland, was given to the British Minister in Stockholm, who gave it to John Mason Neale in 1852. From that copy Neale and Thomas Helmore published songs in two collections, in 1853 and 1854. Neale's "Let the Song be Begun" uses the melody but not the text of the carol.

The carol became more prominent in England after Gustav Holst arranged it for unison voices and orchestra in 1916. With the accompaniment reduced for organ, his version is often used as a processional hymn in churches and cathedrals and often forms part of the Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols; it was sung in the service broadcast from King's College Chapel, Cambridge, in 2011. Holst's setting is sometimes called "Theodoric", after his middle name, Theodore, and under that name it is the tune of Percy Dearmer's hymn "God is love, his the care". The most common English version of the words, "On this day earth shall ring", is by Jane M. Joseph (1894–1929), who published it under the name "James M. Joseph". Elizabeth Poston made another, the "Boys' Carol", in 1965, and the tune was also used for the hymn "Long Ago, Prophets Knew".

Later arrangements include a harmonised choral version by Hugh Keyte and Andrew Parrott in the New Oxford Book of Carols, one by Antony Pitts in the Naxos Book of Carols, two by John Rutter and a Festival Procession by Lara Hoggard with brass, orchestra and organ. Maddy Prior and The Carnival Band recorded it with period instruments on A Tapestry of Carols (1987), and the quartet Anonymous 4 recorded the song with its older "Intonent hodie" text on Legends of St. Nicholas. The jazz musician Wayne Shorter recorded the melody as "12th Century Carol" in 2003.

A soldiers' boast. The song names the heroes of the ancient world and then claims that none of them can match the British grenadiers, who march up to the enemy's walls and throw their grenades under fire, and it ends with a toast to them. The mood is swaggering and cheerful, carried by the beat of the drum.

"White Christmas" was written by Irving Berlin for the 1942 musical film Holiday Inn. Accounts differ as to when and where he wrote it. One story is that he wrote it in 1940 in warm La Quinta, California, while staying at the La Quinta Hotel, a retreat favoured by Hollywood; the Arizona Biltmore also claims the song was written there. Berlin, who often stayed up all night writing, is said to have told his secretary that it was not only the best song he had ever written but the best song anybody had ever written.

Bing Crosby gave the first public performance on his NBC radio show The Kraft Music Hall on Christmas Day 1941, a few weeks after the attack on Pearl Harbor. He recorded it for Decca Records on 29 May 1942, in 18 minutes, with the John Scott Trotter Orchestra and the Ken Darby Singers, and it was released on 30 July in an album of six 78-rpm discs from Holiday Inn. Crosby at first saw nothing special in it. In the film he sings it as a duet with the actress Marjorie Reynolds, whose voice was dubbed by Martha Mears; the original script had Reynolds, not Crosby, singing it. The song won the Academy Award for Best Original Song at the 15th Academy Awards.

It began slowly, overshadowed by another song from the film, but by the end of October 1942 it topped the Your Hit Parade chart, and Crosby's record spent eleven weeks at the top of the Billboard charts that year. It also reached number one on the Harlem Hit Parade for three weeks, Crosby's first appearance on that black-oriented chart. Its mixture of melancholy and comforting images of home has often been said to have spoken especially strongly to listeners during the Second World War, and the Armed Forces Network was flooded with requests for it. Crosby's nephew Howard Crosby recalled his uncle saying that the hardest thing he did in his career was to sing it at an outdoor USO show in northern France in December 1944, with Bob Hope and the Andrews Sisters, before 100,000 soldiers in tears, many of whom were killed in the Battle of the Bulge a few days later.

The record returned to number one in later holiday seasons and reappeared on the pop chart year after year. Because the 1942 master was worn out by use, Crosby recorded the song again on 19 March 1947 with the same orchestra and singers, and with every effort to reproduce the first session; this is the version most often heard on the radio today. The song was used again in the 1954 musical film White Christmas, the highest-grossing film of that year. Crosby's single is credited with sales of at least 50 million copies, which Guinness World Records recognises as the best-selling single of all time; with other versions the song is counted at more than 100 million. More than 500 versions have been recorded, in several languages, among them those of Frank Sinatra in 1944 and of the Drifters, with the lead singer Clyde McPhatter, in 1954.

Writers on popular music see it as a turning point. The song, written by a Jewish immigrant to the United States, showed that secular Christmas songs could succeed commercially; Dave Marsh and Steve Propes wrote that it changed Christmas music by revealing the market for such songs and by establishing the themes of home and nostalgia that run through them. During the Vietnam War a recording was broadcast on Armed Forces Radio on 30 April 1975 as a secret, pre-arranged signal precipitating the U.S. evacuation from Saigon. The 1942 recording entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1974 and was added to the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry in 2002.

text: A light, mocking song about a country fellow who goes to town and thinks a feather in his cap makes him a gentleman. In its first use it laughed at the colonists' lack of polish; the same mockery, taken up by the colonists themselves, became a cheerful boast of plain American pride.
